utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries, therefore the witness can be escorted into the courtroom. Due to my absence of yesterday, I hand over the acting Presidency at this moment to Judge Moloto for the remainder of the testimony of Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to remind you that you're still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Ivetic, you may continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we left off at 65 ter number 1D1114 and I would like to return to that document today as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can have page 4 of the same in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay now, sir, you mentioned yesterday that some of your investigations related to Ovcara and Vukovar and therefore I would like to draw your attention to comment number 4 of this review where the stated medical doctor from New Zealand talks about: "No trenching done in Ovcara. 64 bodies removed in one day to spite a UNTAES photographer. Not all bodies were fluoroscoped." Did you have occasion to be advised of this type of criticism or review of the exhumation work relating to Ovcara as part of your work with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I was, as I said yesterday, aware of the criticisms. I had been aware that it had been dealt with by an inquiry, and that issue I don't recall being raised again in subsequent years.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Based upon your knowledge and training, would you agree with me that fluoroscoping of mortal remains is a very fundamental and important part of the process of removing and examining the remains from a grave as part of a criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. There would be circumstances where you would not, but you would generally do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can turn to the next page of the document, I'd like to focus just on a few more comments, number 12, 13, and 14, if I could draw your attention there, sir. And we have three members of the team, one medical examiner and two anthropologists, there giving some comments. And first of all, the first individual at number 12 says that she complains she was instructed how to list the cause of death by Dr. Kirschner. Is that the type of misconduct that you said you did have knowledge of -- or complaints of misconduct, I should say?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally I believe that that was the major allegation, that the cause of death had been altered; but as I say, I wasn't involved in this process and I only know it peripherally because it was dealt with by the time I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Started --

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- attended The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking at number 13, we see in addition to the complaint that Dr. Kirschner changed autopsy reports and instructed her to do so while processing reports, it says: "In the field, Dr. Haglund dictated too much speed in exhumation." Is that second complaint something that you were aware of as having occurred in the exhumations that were conducted under the head of Dr. Haglund?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Number 14. I would like to direct your attention to the part where this anthropologist says: "Clothing was discarded at Haglund's command, even though some contained identification. Forms were not always used." Were those complaints or criticisms that you were aware of relating to the work of the exhumations that had predated you?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, as part of the exhumations that you did participate in or were present for, how many bodies a day were exhumed on average?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that varied very significantly on the type of grave. If it was an undisturbed grave, a primary undisturbed grave, it might go very quickly. If it was a secondary, disturbed -- a secondary grave, sometimes it was very slow. And sometimes they would uncover a mass of bodies, as you saw in the Kozluk photograph, until they reached a point where they could show the composition of the grave, and then they would remove all those bodies fairly quickly because they were basically ready for removal and left in that position to show the composition of the grave and the relationship between the bodies. It very much depended on the type of grave and the type of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could turn to page 10 of this document. Here, sir, the committee is talking in detail about the unacceptable conduct of Dr. Kirschner in regards to changing the manner of death and autopsies that he himself did not perform, and the discussion is rather serious including talk of losing one's licence or being dismissed, depending on the jurisdiction that was involved. Did you have occasion to learn of such serious discussions about the consequences of Dr. Kirschner's work as part of your employment with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't recall having read this document and I wasn't aware of those discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can go to the next page, page 11. Item number 8 on page 11 confirms that: "There was some validity to the charge of shifting and non-protection of the bones." Was that something that you were aware of when you commenced your work in the field?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and perhaps I'd need to read the rest of the document to see the context. I'm not sure what shifting and non-protection of the bones means in this context, but I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, we have some guide-lines that were suggested by this committee, this review committee, and they're supposed to apply, I guess, for future work of this nature. And I'd like to go through about five or six with you. I'd like to highlight number 2. "Develop uniformity of protocols, diagrams, and abbreviations." To your knowledge, was that recommendation implemented in the subsequent investigations of exhumation sites that you participated in?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Starting from my involvement with Professor Wright, the forms that were used were generally pro formas, including a space for diagrams for the layout of the bodies, et cetera, in a similar vein at the mortuary, and they were amended as the anthropologist or archaeologist in charge saw fit. Predominantly the same form was used over the entire period.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And looking at number 3 it says there there should be a standard UN death certificate. Is that the form that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an autopsy report which detailed the examination of the body or the remains. I think it's perhaps a mis-wording to say a death certificate because the ICTY OTP didn't issue a death certificate. And as I understand the rules, it would have been issued by the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the pro forma document? Was that the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the pro forma document was a report which detailed the autopsy of the individual or the body, so the medical examination of the body or the remains was listed by each anthropologist or forensic dentist or whomever on that form. It included sections for detailing cause of death, what type of examination was conducted, artefacts located. Generally it would have an image of a human skeleton and the author would indicate which parts were perhaps missing or which parts were damaged. And generally that form stayed the same with minor variations across the time I was involved in the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at items number 11 and 12 now. It says: "Develop a system of briefing incoming personnel and debriefing outgoing personnel. Use this as a basis for a good quality assurance program." And number 12: "Develop a quality assurance program for all aspects of the investigation." Were these two recommendations implemented in the exhumation investigations that you participated?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't brief incoming members of the relative experts' teams, but I know that occurred and, in fact, I was present as an observer when that occurred. And I would also at the commencement of a mass grave examination, I would brief the whole team on the processes that we expected and provide a limited amount of information about the mass grave itself, conscious that I didn't want to put a position in their mind beforehand, I would tell them where it was that we had imagery, that we suspected it was connected to Srebrenica, et cetera. As to outgoing interviews, I'm not sure -- I wasn't present when that occurred. I assume that occurred. And I think your last point was quality assurance. I think that's a question for the chief anthropologist and archaeologist. I certainly took a role in examining the artefacts and the documentation and reviewing that for inconsistencies at the level that I could. I'm not an anthropologist or an archaeologist. And I believe that that question should be answered by those experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Who was it that would collect all notes, photographs, radiographs, and other materials from the autopsy?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were at the mortuary at Visoko generally a number of scene -- crime scene officers, generally former or serving police officers. They were responsible at the mortuary for collecting, retaining the physical evidence, which was secured at the mortuary. At regular intervals, I would attend and spend several days to weeks examining that material, partly to link it to the investigation but also to decide what may need further investigation and what may need transport to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: These crime scene officers that you have identified, were they also employees of the Office of the Prosecutor, such as yourself?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to page 13 of this document, item IV is another recommendation by this review panel as to autopsies. It says: "Appoint an independent investigator who would be responsible for initial work and who would report to the legal staff and, subsequently, to an oversight group. Collect all notes, photographs, radiographs and other materials from the autopsy." Can I take it from your previous answer that there was no independent investigator, but rather the persons fulfilling this role were all employees of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd accept that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was an independent investigator ever considered for this role, to your knowledge, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at item number V on this list. "Oversight or review panel of experts (pathologists, anthropologists, odontologists, criminal investigators or other experts deemed necessary). These should not be involved in the incident." To your knowledge were any such recommendations implemented for the exhumations and/or autopsies investigations that you were a part of while at the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe so, although specific examinations were tasked to outside experts, such as soil and watches, et cetera, but not an oversight individual or group.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would tender 1D1114 as the next exhibit in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 1D1114 is admitted into evidence. Maybe it please be given an exhibit number, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1114 receives number D329, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move to some other areas relating to your testimony. I'd like to -- I'd like to discuss with you, sir, your testimony from the Popovic case but it's separate from the testimony that was tendered in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So if we can have 65 ter number 1D1112 in e-court and if we could turn to page 29 of the same in e-court, that should correlate to transcript page 19018 of the underlying transcript. And it is the bottom half of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I'm starting at line 14 and I'll be reading into the record the questions and answers and you can follow along with me, and then I'll have some questions for you about this to see if we can understand this -- if we can confirm this section of your prior -- prior testimony. "Q. [Interpretation] Mr. Manning, please read that sentence as well. "A. 'The majority of information required to submit a detailed report on the Srebrenica examinations' --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "-- exhumations, including a definitive MNI and number of mass graves, is currently held by ICMP.' "Do you wish me to continue? "Q. No. We'll progress gradually. I suppose you stand by this statement made by you in November 2005, that is, two years ago. "A. Yes, I accept that that's a valid statement still. "Q. Thank you. Mr. Manning, could you please read out the following sentence to us, which is actually the continuation of the one you've read out? "A. Your Honours --"

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then we have to go to the top of the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could it be enlarged a little bit further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "'Unfortunately, data held by the various BiH authorities, due to lack of resources or other factors, is widely [Realtime transcript read in error "wild"] spread across agencies and organisations and its accuracy is difficult to assess.' "Q. Thank you. Mr. Manning, would you agree with me that the data you had at your disposal in November 2005 were received from local authorities in Bosnia and that they were incomplete, not up-to-date, and difficult to rely upon? "A. No, I would not agree with that. A significant amount of the data I received was from ICMP, and the various parts of the Bosnia Commission for Missing Persons, some of them records were in excellent condition, some of the records were very detailed, some of the records were perhaps not complete. And also, given my inability to read the language, it was inaccessible to me, given the time-frame. If I'd have had more time to read through the information, I could have made a more appropriate assessment of its accuracy."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, first of all, sir, for this part that we have just gone through, do you stand by this prior testimony as being both truthful and accurate as to the matters raised therein?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, this was at the time of the Popovic trial several years ago. Have you now had more time to read through the information? Have you done that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can -- if I can ask you, first of all, this Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons which is identified in here, am I correct that this is the organisation that at the time was chaired by a Mr. Amor Masovic?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that a Mr. Jasmin Odobasic was an assistant under Mr. Masovic and perhaps later became head of that commission?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not aware of that. I had dealt with Mr. Masovic. And I may have met Mr. Odobasic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Odobasic --

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to -- I apologise. If we can turn to page 35 in e-court which should correlate to transcript page 19024.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before we move on to another section, I just wanted to make a correction to the transcript. Page 10, line 23, currently reads "wild," and I think it should have been and I heard Mr. Ivetic read "widely." Line 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you confirm, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you, Mr. Jeremy. You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go through -- well, first of all, here the discussion is in relation to your preparation of summaries for the year 2007 and the first part is -- well, let me just read it to you from lines 4 to 12, sir, and if you want you can follow along. "Q. So when you were there on that special mission, you were not provided with confidential information, yet now you have told us that when preparing your summaries for the year 2007, in June and November, you had access to confidential information; is this correct? "A. To be clear, I indicated that I did not take copies of confidential material, but I also believe I indicated that I was given access to the material that I wished to view, including the DNA reports, including the exhumation reports, and including the Tuzla Canton Court files." First of all, sir, do you stand by this answer as being truthful and accurate, such that you would so answer again if the same question were asked?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the time that this was going on and you were given access to the confidential information, you were no longer employed by the Office of the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, it was a short-term mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know if the access given to you by the local authorities to confidential information, was that documented by a formal written request from the Tribunal or how did you gain access?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was a formal request made of ICMP and the Bosnian Commission, and on the basis of their acceptance of that, I travelled there and conducted the research.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would you agree with me that neither you nor others from the ICTY Prosecution were present for nor monitored the collection of so-called surface remains from the grave-sites that are identified in your various reports that we -- that were tendered yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you asked if we monitored the collection of surface remains from the grave-sites. If you mean the ICTY exhumed grave-sites, I don't think that's correct. If you mean the additional Bosnian exhumed grave-sites, again there's a distinction between a grave and surface remains, but I can accept that we did not monitor the collection of surface remains and -- except for one season, we did not monitor ICMP and the Bosnian Commission's work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would you agree with me that when -- when your reports rely upon the MNI method of determining victims, that -- the issue of surface remains does not enter into the equation?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The use of the minimal number of individuals count by the anthropologists was based on the remains inside the mass grave, not on surface remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: However, now that we've switched to the ICMP DNA identification method, am I correct that these surface remains from these other investigation efforts by the local authorities do come into the equation?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they come into the equation and they would provide the total number, but there is also indications within the data that shows that some were surface remains and some were removed from mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that, yeah. Would you agree with me that neither you nor anyone at the Prosecution can attest or speak to the procedures that were followed in the collection and preservation and chain of custody of the surface remains?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I examined that process during my 2005 mission, but only superficially, and I examined some of the records and some of the grid references but I didn't go into great detail about the surface remains. I'm not sure if Mr. Janc has or if anyone else has.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'll be sure to check when he comes. Now, did the ICTY do any investigations to determine whether these surface remains dated for the same time-period as the graves themselves, the mass graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And one more question in relation to the ICMP DNA identifications, I think you've already answered it but I'd like to flesh it out. Am I correct that for those exhumations of grave-sites that were conducted by the Bosnian authorities, some of those bodies also come into the figure from the ICMP DNA identification?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, those results would add to the ICMP's total figure. If you're referring to my report from 2007, from memory, without checking the report, the only surface remains or remains that I added from the Bosnian Commission/ICMP work were from Godinjske Bare - pardon my pronunciation - and from the area immediately adjacent to the Kozluk primary mass grave. And I think the Godinjske burials were connected to the Skorpions video or what is known as the Skorpions video.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, perhaps if we can -- perhaps if we can turn to your 2007 report just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe that should be number P1737 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can fresh your recollection, if we can perhaps turn to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the 15th page of the document which -- one page back, actually. I apologise. So I guess it was the 14th page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, at the bottom of this page of your report as to the Hodzici Road 6 - Snagovo 1 location, would you agree that here you have an exhumation conducted by the Bosnian Commission alongside the ICMP without the participation of the ICTY and you do have, at the end, a recitation of the number of individuals that were identified by DNA from this location? Does that refresh your recollection as to whether these figures are included in your 2007 report?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you give your answer, we should wait until the correct page in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- is loaded up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it should be the next page in the B/C/S -- strike that. It's two pages further forward from the B/C/S. One page back apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's still not the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's still not the correct one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The lower part should be that one which correlates to the upper part in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Except that we're at Hodzici Road 4, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you wanted to go to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- lower part -- next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That should make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There we go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, does this refresh your recollection as to whether the bodies exhumed by the Bosnian Commission with ICMP and identified by ICMP constitute a part of your 2007 report?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, now I understand. Yes, that's the case. And in fact, for a number of graves on Hodzici Road, Lipje, Cancari, which were all graves known to the ICTY, probed and tested by the ICTY, were exhumed and DNA analysis conducted by ICMP without ICTY observations. And I used that data for my report, and in fact that was the reason for me attending Bosnia was to gain that data and use in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And now you say here "without ICTY observations." Yesterday you said you could tell looking at the secondary graves whether the person -- persons that were buried in them were part of sanitisation efforts or not based upon various features. For these particular graves alongside Hodzici Road and Cancari, are those secondary graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are secondary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So your testimony yesterday as to how you could exclude those from being graves for sanitisation of bodies would not apply to these graves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe it would. These are secondary graves to the primary mass graves at Ovcara and they showed evidence of executions, witness testimony, blindfolds, et cetera. So these graves are positively linked to the primary graves, and I believe that shows that. But also remembering that these secondary graves were created in September and October of 1995, well after the conflict had ended in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, during your direct examination at transcript page 14157, you said that the focus of the work of the Bosnian Commission and ICMP at the graves was different from yours, and in essence I think you said that the -- their primary motive for the exhumations was to remove the bodies, to have them examined and identified. If I can ask you, is this your position or opinion based upon the information at your disposal about how the BiH Commission was conducting its work?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was based on my understanding of their work and my observations at the grave-sites that they were exhuming. I visited a number, not only when we monitored for one season but also thereafter. And in discussions with ICMP and the Bosnian Commission, their primary goal was to recover the bodies and have them identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct in interpreting these words of yours to mean that the BiH authorities were not as focused nor careful to preserve and document other artefacts or evidence recovered from the graves, but rather were just focused on getting the remains out and identified as quickly as possible?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was their focus. However, I was aware that not only ICMP but the Bosnian Commission, if possible, would recover artefacts; if possible, would recover data from the mass graves. And that the ICMP produced exhumation or examination reports from the graves in an attempt to show how they were made, what artefacts may have been in them. But the primary focus was to get the bodies out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you believe, sir, that this methodology employed by the BiH Commission as to the exhumations leads to less diligence in following standard protocols and procedures for documenting the evidence and preserving the evidence from potential contamination?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that's not a question for me, but their focus was not to collect evidence. Their focus was to remove the bodies. As I say, that may be a question for someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the next several questions, I believe we need to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Mr. Manning, we'll take a break for 20 minutes and we'll come back a little later at 10 to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we take a break and come back at 10 to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to re-visit one other thing from your prior testimony in the Popovic case at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter number 1D1111 in e-court. It should be page 55 of the same, and it should be the last two lines and it will be bleeding on to the next page, the first four lines of the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, again, please feel free to follow along with me beginning at line 24. "Q. Okay. And, generally, how were you able to tell that the bodies were from 1995 and not from some other time?" And if we can go to the next page and zoom in on lines 1 through 4. "A. We, of course, relied on the creation date of the mass grave, that the graves had been created in July of 1995, or had been created thereafter in September and October 1995. So they couldn't pre-date 1995, in July." Do you stand by this part of your prior testimony as being truthful and accurate, sir?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that this approach that you utilise is an assumption, that basically all the secondary graves that you identify as coming into existence in September and October of 1995 are actually filled with the remains or bodies from graves that were dated from July 1995? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't believe it's an assumption. It was a fact as to their creation dates. We still on the opening of every grave sought to prove or disprove that that grave was connected to Srebrenica. We approached it with an open mind looking for that confirmation or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that confirmation is found in the next paragraph of your testimony, where you further explain identifying items that you found on the bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that my transcript is not working. Is the main transcript working?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you have to do a few exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Connect again because it was disconnected for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can perhaps -- to be fair to the witness and to have the record full, I can also read the following two paragraphs that are the continuation of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Quote from line 5: "We also -- we also looked at identification material found amongst the bodies. We would find identifications indicating the individuals were from Srebrenica, and often we could find those identifications indicating the persons were recorded as missing from Srebrenica in the ICRC Book of the Missing. "There were also other links which indicated a strong connection to Srebrenica, and therefore the time, including Dutch newspapers from 1995, Dutch medical military rations, Dutch artifacts, as well as artifacts which linked individuals to Srebrenica itself or to Potocari." Sir, does this full answer that I've now read -- first of all, is it truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does that complete your answer as to how -- as to why you believe that the working thesis that the bodies could not predate July of 1995 is not an assumption, in your view?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and backed up by the subsequent DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you - and by "you," I mean you or other personnel at the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal - do any investigations to determine if, in fact, this thesis, which I call an assumption, was true, that none of the bodies in the secondary graves could have predated July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I seek clarification?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You started your questioning with quoting the witness, where you said: "We ... relied on the creation date of the mass grave, that the graves had been created in July of 1995, or had been created thereafter in September and October 1995. So they couldn't predate 1995 ..." Now, that is about graves and mass graves. You're now talking about no person possibly being in one of these graves, a person, if I take it, which died before July 1995. Now, the -- I'm just trying to follow you. If you find a person in a grave who is reported as still being alive in July and then went missing and then ends up in that grave, that would -- that's at least my logic but please explore with the witness whether I'm wrong, that would suggest that at least that grave was filled up with at least that person and perhaps more persons who died in or after mid-July 1995. Now, the question of whether there may have been a body of a person who died earlier is a different question. Whether another person -- whether that grave existed already before July 1995 and then was filled up with persons who died in July 1995, persons in a grave and the creation of a grave are two different questions. If you would -- that's at least my understanding. And you started with the graves and you ended up with bodies --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honours, if we can go to the previous page of the document, the beginning of the question that I quoted talks about bodies, and that might be the confusion Your Honours have, lines 24 and 25 of the prior page of the transcript which is where I began reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me have a look and that is at --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, that's at page 55, lines 24 through 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you read it -- well, there he says "often," isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Other time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it in our transcript where you put it to the witness. Yes, let me see. You read to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I read at page -- I apologise, it should be at page 27, line 8, is where I begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 27, line 8 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You began at line 24 -- oh, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about now, today's transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is line 24 of the document which is 1D1111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that the question is: "And, generally, were you able to tell that the bodies were from 1995 and not from some other time?" And then the witness said something about the graves, so there is some disparity in question and answer and that's perhaps exactly what I was referring to. And you then finally -- "whether any investigations were done to determine if, in fact, this thesis, which I call an assumption, was true that none of the bodies in the secondary" -- you now turn to the negative. It's logically not concluded. No reason not to further explore the matter, but I'm just pointing at the -- at the analytical flaws in the, perhaps, line of questioning and answers previous case, this case, so that it becomes clear at least now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I may proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us, did you do - I say "you," yourself and the Office of the Prosecutor - any investigations to determine if any bodies that predated July of 1995 could have potentially have been buried in the secondary graves that were dug in September and October of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, Your Honours, we examined each body removed from the grave with that view. Not only was the first body or the 100th body connected to Srebrenica, we would look for that evidence. And there were investigations undertaken by the Srebrenica team, such as interviewing witnesses and suspects, including the men who drove the buses and backhoes and machinery that created the graves to try and establish if those bodies were from Srebrenica when they were created. We looked at vehicle logs, et cetera. So there were investigations around that issue as to when the graves were created and who was in the graves. I don't recall any information that indicated there was someone from a previous era in any of the graves. That may have changed since I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, we have evidence in this case, in particular transcript page 11481 through 11482, from Witness RM306 who testified that a communal grave of 100 to 150 bodies dating from 1992 and buried in a communal grave at Bratunac in 1992 after an investigation involving a forensic pathologist, that these graves were dug up by Mr. Momir Nikolic in autumn of 1995 and that this information was communicated to your predecessor, Mr. Jean Rene Ruez. Did you know about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I may have heard that allegation. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, if true, wouldn't this basically be something that would need to take into account in relation to the accuracy of your working thesis, which I call an assumption?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't recall that allegation, as I said, and I don't know if that allegation was investigated. I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As you sit here today as a witness, can you exclude 100 per cent the possibility that at least 100 to 150 bodies from 1992 were reburied in one of the secondary mass graves dating from September and October of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my knowledge of the exhumation and autopsy process, I believe that could be excluded. I don't believe that's the case. And if that was the case, those records would be definitively shown by the DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you if you have any knowledge or information of a process known as "asanacija" or sanitisation which was prescribed under the laws of the former SFRY and employed by all three sides to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to "asanacija," or the removing of dead carcasses of animals, ordnance, and bodies of killed combatants from the terrain so as to dispose or bury the same, would that process, if you know, include cloth, fabrics or clothing found in the battle-field?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me would cloth and clothing be collected, I don't know if I can answer that. My understanding of "asanacija" is the removal predominantly of human remains or the burial of human remains as a sanitary measure. Would they collect their clothing that was on the bodies? I assume so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, in relation to battle-field casualties of the Bosnian Muslim column that departed from Srebrenica in July of 1995, there are various sources that indicate that up to 3.000 column members were killed in combat or by going through minefields. There is a UN Secretary-General's report dated 15 November 1999 based upon interviews with survivors of the column. There is also a 17 July 1995 report of the UN Civil Protection Affairs Office that also quotes a figure of up to 3.000 members of the Bosnian Muslim column that had become deceased as a result of combat or mines. Did your investigation offer any insight as to the number of combat and mine-related casualties suffered by the Bosnian Muslim column that was leaving Srebrenica and attempting to break through to Muslim territory in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not directly involved in that aspect. That was mainly the military analyst -- analyst on the team. I did take statements from individuals about that process. I was generally aware of it. I can't at this stage give you the numbers that may have been killed in the column, but I accept that there was fighting, and in some cases I understand quite violent fighting, and that a number of individuals were killed, which may be reflected in the collection of surface remains by ICMP and the Bosnian Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Richard Butler in the Popovic trial at transcript page 20251 conceded that 1.000 to 2.000 dead from combat engagements by the column was reasonable. Is that individual the military analyst that you have just identified in your answer at lines 12 and 13 of today's transcript?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is, amongst others. And I would accept that figure from Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Dusan Janc - you've mentioned him a couple times in your testimony - during the Popovic trial at transcript pages 33543 to 33545 said that he could not exclude the possibility that other bodies were buried at secondary graves in addition to murder victims. Do you dispute that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't here to hear his testimony. My belief is that we did not have evidence of that, and I note that Mr. Janc has been working on that -- on the DNA since I've left and I can't comment on his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say that he's been working on it since you left. Do you know of a -- of -- have you had knowledge of his report that was authored, I believe, in 2009? Have you had a chance to become familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read a report from Dusan in perhaps 2007. I don't believe I've read one since. I haven't kept up with the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the report of Mr. Janc that you read indicate that only 6 per cent of secondary grave corpses could be matched by DNA to primary graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I would be very surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- you're putting reports to the witness. Do we have them in evidence or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We don't yet. Mr. Janc is, I believe, scheduled to be a forthcoming witness in this case. He has not testified yet in this proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because to understand fully what he means by only 6 per cent of secondary grave corpses could be matched by DNA to primary graves, which -- what -- in the context of that report, I take it that an explanation will be given. It would mean, may I take it, that in 6 per cent of the cases that bodily remains were found in the primary graves, where bodily remains with the same DNA were found in the secondary graves. So every body which is fully transported from the primary grave to the secondary grave --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which is -- so therefore, I'm just thinking about whether there is any suggestion in your question that the bodies cannot be linked or is it just by the DNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The way I'm reading the report is the exact same way as Your Honour has just summarised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that means that for 6 per cent of --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- dissociated bodies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- dissociated -- that it could be linked, and of course it's the position of the Defence that if the body is not dissociated, that you would not -- no, let me say, if the body is complete and if it would be completely transported from the primary grave to the secondary grave, you would not find any DNA support for that operation, no linkage in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear to me and now -- perhaps it was clear to everyone already, but it's clear to me now as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I did not want to bring Mr. Janc's report because I know it was in 2009 and that's why I first asked the witness if he reviewed it and that's why I wanted to see if -- which report he's talking about, if it was the same one or not, and I can't tell so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, of course, the discussion will be whether 6 per cent is much or little.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll have many discussions, I'm sure, on that topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is the issue which will then need to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can briefly pull up P1481, page 7. And if I've done my counting of the pages right, that should be the map which we had yesterday in hard copy that I don't know if everyone still has. And if the witness needs a copy, he can have -- with the help of the usher, if we could have the witness be given the copy that Madam Stewart is offering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is the map you talked about yesterday that I believe you had created in relation to the secondary graves, and one I -- one question I wanted to ask you about this is: Looking at the secondary graves, especially the ones that are alongside the road, which I believe would be the Hodzici mass grave sites, based upon the information, the totality of the information, that you and the Office of the Prosecutor had at your disposal about the movements of the 5th column -- pardon me, not the 5th column, the column of Bosnian men from Srebrenica, would you agree with me that all of these secondary graves are located 5 kilometres or closer from the sites of reported and known combat engagements of that column of Bosnian males?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't say that. I would have to check the records, and as I say, I wasn't heavily involved in the investigation of the column and its path. But I would have to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know that, sir. But yesterday I believe you testified that these were all far away from battle-fields. So I'm trying to understand the basis of your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I was asked if it was 5 kilometres. I can't confirm that. To my knowledge and having been there, there was no sign of any battle within the area, particularly along Hodzici Road. It's completely -- or was completely abandoned and in a remote location.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to -- well, I don't want to go through all of your reports, so maybe I'll just deal with one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So if we can pull up P1738 MFI, a 2003 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for that, I would like to ask you a general question. Can we agree that the material that's contained in your reports at all times is simply reciting or summarising what you believe the results of the experts and others who examined materials were reporting?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's not correct. Yes, I examined the expert reports. I took data from those expert reports. But as I said yesterday, because the project was so long and was involving a number of personnel, some of the reports from the experts did not cover the whole period, they did not cover the developments within the investigations. I examined the autopsy reports. I examined the blindfolds and ligatures, the physical artefacts, the connections, the identifications. And I checked each and every fact within the expert reports and sought to confirm if we did, indeed, have autopsy reports which indicated a cause of death in agreement with that expert report. But as I said yesterday, in examining the blindfolds and ligatures, for instance, I did that work and that is reported in my reports, and that is work that I produced and that reflects the examination of the total material available to us from exhumations over a significant period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 3 of the English, page 4 of the B/C/S or Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And there at the top in the English and it's at the top in the B/C/S we have the cause of death that you have just, I believe, mentioned in your answer. And I want to ask you in terms of these cases here, is this related only to those bodies identified by DNA or is it also in relation to the other bodies that were exhumed and that are identified as unique DNA signatures whose actual name and date of birth have not been identified, if you can follow that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you may have to ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask it this way. The statistics contained in this section of your report, do they relate to the entirety of bodies that were identified as having a unique DNA signature, including those for whom the DNA testing has not yet determined their actual name and identity?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage of the investigation, the DNA results were not available predominantly, and these figures represent the examination of the bodies at the mortuary and the findings of the pathologist. It's not an examination of the DNA of those individuals or their uniqueness. And in that time, the minimal number of individuals count was performed by Mr. Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as to those that are listed as having died of undetermined cause, can you please tell me, if you know, what was the -- what was the standard procedure under the law in the former Yugoslavia for cases where there was a determination of an undetermined cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that law from the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could I then ask the following. The cause of death as presented here, was that the cause of death as established under the law of the former Yugoslavia or was it a finding of the investigation's?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was a finding by the chief pathologist and anthropologist based on an examination of the remains. So they were presenting a cause of death of the remains that they're able to examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you say "chief pathologist," you are referring to ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. John Clark and Dr. Chris Lawrence and also the anthropologist Jose Pablo Baraybar. So these figures represent the results of the autopsy process and their understanding as to why those individuals or those parts of those individuals were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned the chief pathologist, you've mentioned Dr. Clark, Dr. Lawrence, and anthropologist Baraybar. Just -- least we forget, am I correct that Dr. William Kirschner was also chief pathologist for some of these?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I would also indicate Professor Haglund or Dr. Haglund.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, as to the remaining statistics that you give, I see that the vast majority are confirmed and -- as probably gun-shots and also actual gun-shots and then blast injuries is also a category for which both probable and ascertained are the bulk of the statistics. Now, did your investigation consider at all the possibility that certain persons who became deceased as a result of these two causes became deceased as part of the column of Srebrenica males attempting to break through the Serb lines through Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That possibility was considered, and I had many conversations with the experts in relation to the cause of death and how they could ascertain that. It was considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now what about considering the possibility that certain persons came to be deceased as the result of suicide, whether by fire-arms or by grenade, rather than to end up being captured by the Serbs. Did your research and investigation take into account that possibility?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that was considered in terms of how the individuals died. Was it suicide or were they, in fact, shot. And as I say, I had discussions with the experts about how the individuals were killed, how they could show that, and what that told them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to put something to you and see what you say to that. I put it to you, sir, that people wishing to exploit battle-field "asanacija" or sanitisation actions that occurred in the weeks and months following the fighting may have placed the remains of execution victims taken from primary graves in these graves that were meant for battle-field casualties. Can you exclude that possibility 100 per cent in your view?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Ivetic, are you asking the witness to exclude a possibility or are you putting what you -- an assertion to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm putting an assertion. That's my assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with the possibility of that assertion, sir?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you this, sir: On the territory of Zvornik and Bratunac municipalities, did you - and, again, when I say "you," I don't mean you personally, I mean yourself along with other personnel from the Office of the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to have to take you back to that question, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said -- you call it an assertion, but you say "may have placed," that cannot be an assertion. There's still a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I meant to say "placed," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You meant to say "placed."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Placed. As part of my assertion to the witness that persons did, in fact, place execution victims from the primary mass graves in graves that also had battle-field casualties that were collected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you're correcting that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, the question I now have for you is: Isn't it correct that you - that is, yourself and other personnel from the Office of the Prosecutor - in fact, did a fairly diligent and comprehensive investigation to scour the terrain of both Zvornik and Bratunac, looking for any possible mass graves that could exist?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did look for mass graves. We used the aerial imagery. We were trying to find any other mass graves, particularly obviously connected to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as part of that process, did you not also interview persons that would have been involved in the "asanacija" or sanitisation activities, such as grave diggers, public sanitation, or civil protection departments and the like?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we interviewed individuals who were involved in the creation of the primary mass graves and the creation of the secondary mass graves who transported the bodies that they had dug up and placed them in those graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you agree with me that those bodies that would have been the result of battle-field casualties and that would have been, therefore, the subject of sanitisation activities, whatever their number, I'm not now talking about the numbers, whatever their number, they would have to have been buried somewhere? They don't just evaporate into thin air. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe - and I'm conscious that I didn't directly investigate the matter at length - I believe that the majority of the individuals killed in the battle and in the column were left to decompose, and eventually they were collected by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons. I do not recall seeing evidence of a large-scale or systematic recovery of the bodies by Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a different question. Did you find any graves that would have been sanitisation graves, distinct and apart from the graves that you did find that you say are all related to execution victims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And how would the sanitisation graves be identifiable, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Those having bodies that were not victims of executions that would have been dug by sanitisation personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I'm saying is when you find a grave there, how do you determine that this is a sanitisation grave?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: By doing investigations. So if after the investigations did they determine that any graves that they had located were sanitisation graves. I apologise, Your Honour. Thank you for correcting me in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not and the graves that we examined and exhumed were found to be connected to Srebrenica and the execution of the individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question in this context?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you believed that combat casualties would just have been left and not -- sanitation would not have probably taken place, which would result in, I take it, bodily remains to be found wherever, not necessarily in graves. Do you have any knowledge about the -- if I could say the incidental bodies found here and there as a result of non-sanitised combat casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was aware that remains were collected by the Bosnian Commission over several years, and in 2005 when I examined their records and went to their offices, they provided me details of the number of bodies that they had collected and the very broad areas that they had collected them. They would travel through the woods, through the areas of the column, and collect either individual skeletons or more probably parts of individuals that had been scavenged by animals. And they would collect those remains up and they would be termed as surface remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And are there records of that -- I'm perhaps not only looking in your direction, Mr. Witness, but also partly to Mr. Jeremy, Mr. Groome. Are there records of the numbers of bodies found not necessarily in graves?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, there are, Your Honours, particularly in the 2007 report of Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the 2007 report, sir, with respect to these so-called surface remains, aren't most of them at or near the secondary grave sites that were exhumed by the BiH Commission?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, we had a witness that testified about Bratunac, RM306, and in relation to the so-called Glogova mass grave on that territory. And he confirmed at transcript pages 11452 to 11453 that bodies that were recovered by the civil protection staff as part of sanitisation that were found at -- along the roadway were, in fact, buried at Glogova alongside those persons deceased in Kravica and other locations. Is that something that you knew as part of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that. I understand since I've left that there's been some developments in where -- in relation to Glogova, and I do recall grave L of Glogova which is probably a separate incident to Kravica but connected to Srebrenica and an execution. But I haven't kept up with the investigations since I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we've also had several witnesses at this trial, Bosnian Muslim males, who were part of the column who have testified about casualties inflicted on the column by Serb troops during the attempted break through, including the use of shelling and fire-arms; those would be RM253 and RM254. We have also had evidence from some of the same witnesses that persons were committing suicide, including by the use of hand-grenades and also by the instance of family members shooting each other simultaneously. Did you come across such information as part of your investigative work?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I recall reading such statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, forensically speaking, at the autopsy table one cannot exclude or differentiate the damage caused by these battle-field casualties or the suicides from the deaths caused by execution, I'm talking about the damage to the remains, physical damage?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm conscious that I'm not a forensic expert, pathologist. From my experience in investigations, hopefully you could tell that to a degree depending on circumstances. If the individuals were standing together and opened a grenade, the injuries would be different than having one thrown at them. If they were shot in the head with a blindfold, that would be an indication of an execution. But there are, I'm sure, instances where you could not tell the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question in the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- area. We have a large number of individuals died of undetermined causes. Now, are ligatures and blindfolds found also on those persons for whom the cause of death could not be determined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd specifically have to check, but yes, I think that is the case. And to give you an example, there may be an arm recovered with a ligature placed around the wrists. Now, the rest of the body is missing, particularly given the period of this report. So you have a dissociated human arm with a ligature around the wrist, and the rest of the body is not present. Therefore, they could not establish a cause of death of that individual; however, there is a strong indication that that person has been executed or at least bound before they were killed. And later on in the process you may discover, particularly through DNA, that the rest of that body is in a secondary grave. You could then - and I have seen them do this at the Bosnian Commission - you physically put the arm back with the body and you now have an individual who was perhaps killed and executed and you have the ligature attached to that body now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, let me follow-up on Your Honour's question. We see here several thousand individuals in total from these various causes of death and the question was about ligatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to call up P1735 MFI and turn to page 4 in the English and 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is something that you went through yesterday, I believe, in direct examination and that I believe you indicated that you had prepared based upon your own work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, it's P1735 MFI. And it will be page 4 of that exhibit or, excuse me, MFI'd exhibit. I apologise, it's my mistake. P1734.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document is a one-page document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then let's have the first page -- the one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we -- yeah, this is I think the one. If we look at this, is it -- these are the numbers you talked about yesterday, I believe. 440 approximately -- 448 blindfolds that you could conclude conclusively were found in the graves. Am I correct that your further investigation found that approximately 298 were, in fact, attached either around the head or the face?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And as to the ligatures, we see here the number 425, that would be the total number that you conclusively confirmed could be linked to the graves?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise, 423.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct, then, that the column indicates that 327 of those would have been discovered attached to wrists or arms of remains?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to P1735 MFI, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at item number 2 from the exhumation events in 2000, we have in this particular grave a determination of a minimum number of 17 individuals being buried therein. It is reported eight of the 17 had blindfolds and 32 additional blindfolds were found loose in the grave. Would these 32 additional blindfolds that could not be linked to these 17 bodies be included in the total figures for blindfolds that we just went through on your chart?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's a summary of the table that across all the graves 117 were found loose in the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that would mean that 117 of the 442 or 48 -- 140-something would have been found loose in various of the graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to page 7 in both versions of this document that we have in e-court, P1735 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at -- if we look at the entry under blindfolds that's for 4th April, 1996, it talks about certain blindfolds that appeared similar to those found in graves but that were found outside of the graves at a dump site and the investigators did not retain these. Why was the decision made not to preserve these blindfolds that were found outside of the grave for which -- I don't know whether it's you or someone else has made the determination that they were substantially similar to the ones found in the graves? Who made the decision not to preserve this evidence?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wasn't with the OTP at that stage. I'm aware that team leader Jean Rene Ruez located those items. He filmed and videotaped them. It was in late -- it was in early 1996, and I understand from speaking with Mr. Ruez why he didn't retain those items. He retained a small number from Grbavci school, but he didn't retain the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, I think we're getting ahead of ourselves. I believe Grbavci school is the 11th April, 1996, the following paragraph, where it does say that a representative sample of 12 blindfolds was taken. Are you linking these two events separated by seven days as being the same, or was Mr. Ruez talking about both or one?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was talking about the same issue. The Grbavci school and the Orahovac primary execution points are linked and he explained to me the location of those blindfolds at the Grbavci school and also at the rubbish dump at Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you -- the opinions stated in this report that they were similar or indistinguishable from those found in the graves, whose opinion or assertation is that which you are reporting in your report?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a degree it is Dr. Maljaars, Suzi Maljaars from the Netherlands Forensic Institute. It also represents the comments by the chief pathologist and archeologist. And Dr. Maljaars examined those blindfolds and established links. And it also is my opinion from an examination of those items which are represented in photographs of each of the items.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 10 of this document, you indicated that Ms. Maljaars was the source for some of that. And at page 10, as to blindfolds you'll see for the -- let me just read the passage for you. It says: "The blindfolds recovered from the Lazete 2C site have not been

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: majority of the blindfolds located within the grave are indistinguishable from those located in the Lazete 2A & B, Lazete 1, and the related secondary sites of Hodzici Road 3, Hodzici Road 4, and Hodzici Road 5." In relation to these blindfolds that are identified in this paragraph, am I correct you could not have relied upon Ms. Maljaars?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I indicated that Ms. Maljaars was part of that reliance. From the other experts, chief anthropologist, archaeologist, and from my own examination.

utterances.speaker: THE NETHERLANDS FORENSIC INSTITUTE
utterances.text: And which one is this? Is this from your own examination or is it from relying upon one of the experts?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of those.

utterances.speaker: THE NETHERLANDS FORENSIC INSTITUTE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in relation to your reports, you summarise in some of them the findings of soil and pollen experts. Were those soil and pollen expert reports sought by the Prosecution for purposes of being used in trials at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it was one expert, Dr. Anthony Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE NETHERLANDS FORENSIC INSTITUTE
utterances.text: And he was a professor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: A professor from Exeter University, if memory serves me.

utterances.speaker: THE NETHERLANDS FORENSIC INSTITUTE
utterances.text: That's correct, I think. And your report also cites the results of blood and tissue testing done by the United States Naval Criminal Investigation Service, or NCIS. Were those expert reports sought by the Prosecution from the NCIS for purposes of using the same at trial before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were sought. I don't recall that being the reason they examined the sites because it was very early on, but they did seek the report or reports.

utterances.speaker: THE NETHERLANDS FORENSIC INSTITUTE
utterances.text: And your reports also mention a review by explosives experts. Were those reports sought by the Prosecution for purposes of using them at these trials here at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: THE NETHERLANDS FORENSIC INSTITUTE
utterances.text: And I want to ask you, sir, in relation to the soil and pollen, the blood and tissue, and the explosives testing that we've just gone through, did you personally participate in any of the testing or was that all done by these other entities or persons whom we have just now identified in the last couple of minutes?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
